learn: Why retrieval complements a model's parametric knowledge
The retriever–generator (RAG) framework: index, retrieve, augment, generate
Dense retrieval with embeddings and cosine similarity
BM25 keyword retrieval and hybrid fusion
Retrieval over tables and semi-structured data
intro.why: RAG is the most widely deployed LLM pattern in industry: it grounds answers in current, private documents, adds citations, and is far cheaper to update than fine-tuning.

sections.title: Why retrieval
sections.plain: Look things up at question time instead of relying only on what the model memorised.
sections.body:
An LLM's parametric knowledge is frozen at training time, compressed and imprecise. It cannot know recent events or private documents, and it may hallucinate plausible details. Retrieval-augmented generation supplies non-parametric knowledge: relevant passages are fetched at query time and placed in the prompt.

Benefits: current and private knowledge without retraining; answers grounded in sources with citations; easy updates and deletions (edit the index); access control per document. It is like an open-book exam: the model still needs to read and reason, but it no longer has to remember everything. Compared with fine-tuning, RAG is better for facts, while fine-tuning is better for behaviour and format (M7).

sections.title: The retriever–generator framework
sections.plain: Prepare the documents once; then for each question, fetch the best passages and let the model answer from them.
sections.body:
Offline indexing: load documents → clean and chunk → embed each chunk (and/or build a keyword index) → store vectors with metadata (source, date, permissions) in a vector database.

Online: (1) retrieve the top-k chunks for the query (dense, keyword or hybrid, optionally reranked); (2) augment the prompt with numbered chunks and instructions ("answer only from the context; cite sources; say if unknown"); (3) generate.

Failures can arise at each stage: relevant text never indexed, poor chunking, retrieval misses (low recall), irrelevant chunks distracting the model (low precision), or the generator ignoring or contradicting the context. Evaluate retrieval and generation separately (M14).

sections.title: Dense retrieval and cosine similarity
sections.plain: Turn texts into vectors that point the same way when they mean similar things, and find the closest ones.
sections.body:
An embedding model (often a bi-encoder trained with contrastive learning) maps queries and chunks into the same vector space. Relevance is measured by cosine similarity:

$$\cos(q,d) = \frac{q\cdot d}{\lVert q\rVert\,\lVert d\rVert}$$

Worked: q = (1, 2), d = (2, 1): 4 / (√5 · √5) = 0.80. With normalised vectors cosine equals the dot product. Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes (HNSW graphs, IVF clusters, product quantization) find the top-k among millions of vectors in milliseconds.

Dense retrieval captures paraphrases ("money back" ≈ "refund") but can miss exact identifiers, rare names and numbers, and depends on the embedding model's domain.

sections.title: BM25 and hybrid retrieval
sections.plain: Keyword search scores exact word matches, favouring rare words; combine it with vector search to get the best of both.
sections.body:
BM25 is the classic sparse (keyword) ranking function:

$$\text{BM25}(q,d)=\sum_{w\in q}\text{IDF}(w)\frac{f(w,d)(k_1+1)}{f(w,d)+k_1\big(1-b+b\frac{|d|}{\text{avgdl}}\big)}$$

IDF rewards rare terms; k₁ (≈1.2–2) saturates repeated terms; b (≈0.75) normalises for length. It excels at exact matches (codes like "E42", names) and needs no training, but misses synonyms.

Hybrid retrieval runs both and fuses results, commonly with reciprocal rank fusion: score = Σ 1/(60 + rank). In ex1, "refund period" gets no BM25 match (refund ≠ refunds) but dense finds it; "money back" is found by BM25 while the toy dense model errs; hybrid gets both right.

sections.title: Chunking strategies
sections.plain: Cut documents into pieces of the right size, without slicing facts in half.
sections.body:
Chunks are the unit of retrieval. Strategies:

  • Fixed-size (tokens or words): simple; boundaries may split a fact. In ex2, 12-word chunks split the refund sentence across two chunks.
  • Sliding window with overlap: repeats some words between neighbours so boundary facts appear whole in at least one chunk.
  • Structure-aware / recursive: split by headings, paragraphs, then sentences (ex2's three section chunks are each self-contained).
  • Semantic: split where embedding similarity between consecutive sentences drops.

Trade-offs: small chunks are precise but lose context; large chunks dilute embeddings and consume prompt space. Typical sizes are a few hundred tokens with 10–20% overlap; attach titles and metadata, or retrieve small chunks but feed their parent section.

sections.title: Reranking
sections.plain: Fetch many candidates quickly, then use a slower, smarter model to put the best ones first.
sections.body:
Bi-encoders and BM25 score query and chunk independently, which is fast but coarse. A reranker, usually a cross-encoder that reads query and chunk together, scores each candidate more accurately. Pipeline: retrieve top 50–100 → rerank → keep top 3–10 for the prompt.

In ex2, word overlap ranks the returns policy first for "how many days until my refund arrives"; the reranker promotes the refund-timing passage. Rerankers improve precision at small k, reduce distracting context ("lost in the middle" effects) and prompt cost, at the price of extra latency. LLMs themselves can act as rerankers. Diversity (avoiding near-duplicates, e.g. maximal marginal relevance) also matters.

sections.title: Tabular and semi-structured RAG
sections.plain: For tables, translate the question into a query and compute the answer instead of searching text.
sections.body:
Questions over tables need filtering, joining and aggregation, which similarity search cannot do. Approaches:

  • Text-to-SQL / code: the LLM writes a query from the schema, it is executed, and the result is phrased as an answer (ex2: WHERE quarter = 'Q2' ORDER BY sales → Chennai, 175; Pune total 270).
  • Table summaries: index a description of each table (columns, meaning) to route questions to the right table.
  • Semi-structured documents: parse reports and documents into text and tables separately; keep table structure (headers, units) rather than flattening into prose.

Guardrails: read-only database users, query validation, row limits and showing the query for transparency. These ideas lead directly into data-analysis agents (M13).

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Long context doesn't replace RAG: stuffing everything is costly and models use mid-context information less reliably.
  • Query rewriting (expanding, decomposing, or generating a hypothetical answer to embed) often improves recall.
  • GraphRAG builds entity graphs for multi-hop and corpus-wide questions.
  • Citations need checking: a model can cite a source that doesn't support its claim; evaluate faithfulness (M14).

code.title: Cosine, BM25, dense and hybrid retrieval
code.explain: Computes cosine((1,2),(2,1)) = 0.80, implements BM25 over five support documents, builds a toy dense encoder from character trigrams, and fuses both rankings with reciprocal rank fusion, showing each method failing on a different query while hybrid succeeds on all three.
mistakes: Using raw dot products with unnormalised vectors.
Expecting BM25 to match morphological variants.
code.notes: A trained embedding model would replace the trigram encoder.
code.code:
"""Cosine similarity, BM25, a simple dense retriever, and hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion."""
import math, re, zlib
import numpy as np

a, b = np.array([1, 2]), np.array([2, 1])
print(f"cosine((1,2),(2,1)) = {a@b} / ({np.linalg.norm(a):.3f} x {np.linalg.norm(b):.3f}) = {a@b/(np.linalg.norm(a)*np.linalg.norm(b)):.2f}")

docs = ["Refunds are issued within 14 days of a return request.",
        "To reset your password, open Settings and choose Security.",
        "Our office in Pune is open Monday to Friday.",
        "Error code E42 means the payment card was declined.",
        "Money back is possible for two weeks after purchase."]
tok = lambda s: re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", s.lower())
D = [tok(d) for d in docs]; N = len(D); avg = sum(map(len, D)) / N
df = {}
for d in D:
    for w in set(d): df[w] = df.get(w, 0) + 1
def bm25(q, d, k1=1.5, b=0.75):
    s = 0.0
    for w in tok(q):
        if w not in df: continue
        idf = math.log(1 + (N - df[w] + 0.5) / (df[w] + 0.5))
        f = d.count(w)
        s += idf * f * (k1 + 1) / (f + k1 * (1 - b + b * len(d) / avg))
    return s

# A toy "dense" encoder: character trigrams hashed into 64 dimensions (captures partial word overlap)
def embed(s, dim=64):
    v = np.zeros(dim)
    for w in tok(s):
        w = f"#{w}#"
        for i in range(len(w) - 2): v[zlib.crc32(w[i:i+3].encode()) % dim] += 1
    return v / (np.linalg.norm(v) + 1e-9)
E = np.array([embed(d) for d in docs])

for q in ("refund period", "error E42", "how long to get my money back"):
    bm = [bm25(q, d) for d in D]
    dn = E @ embed(q)
    rb, rd = np.argsort(bm)[::-1], np.argsort(dn)[::-1]
    rb = [i for i in rb if bm[i] > 0]                       # BM25 only ranks documents sharing a term
    rrf = {i: (1/(60 + rb.index(i) + 1) if i in rb else 0) + 1/(60 + list(rd).index(i) + 1) for i in range(N)}
    hy = sorted(rrf, key=rrf.get, reverse=True)
    print(f"\nquery: {q!r}")
    print(f"  BM25 top  : " + (f"doc {rb[0]} (score {bm[rb[0]]:.2f})" if rb else "no document shares a term (refund vs refunds)"))
    print(f"  dense top : doc {rd[0]} (cosine {dn[rd[0]]:.2f})")
    print(f"  hybrid RRF: doc {hy[0]} -> {docs[hy[0]]}")

code.title: Chunking, reranking, prompt assembly and tables
code.explain: Compares fixed-size chunks (with and without overlap) to structure-aware chunks, reranks first-stage candidates so the refund-timing passage comes first, assembles a grounded prompt with a citation instruction, and answers table questions by filtering and aggregating (Chennai 175; Pune 270).
mistakes: Embedding table rows and hoping similarity does arithmetic.
code.notes: The reranker is a simple stand-in for a cross-encoder.
code.code:
"""Chunking strategies, reranking retrieved chunks, assembling a grounded prompt, and tabular retrieval."""
import re

doc = ("Returns. Items can be returned within 30 days. Electronics must be unopened. "
       "Refunds. Refunds are paid to the original card within 14 days of receiving the item. "
       "Shipping. Standard delivery takes 3 to 5 days. Express delivery takes 1 day.")
words = doc.split()

def fixed(words, size, overlap):
    step = size - overlap
    return [" ".join(words[i:i+size]) for i in range(0, max(1, len(words) - overlap), step)]
for size, ov in ((12, 0), (12, 4)):
    ch = fixed(words, size, ov)
    print(f"fixed {size} words, overlap {ov}: {len(ch)} chunks; chunk 2 = {ch[1]!r}")
sentences = re.split(r"(?<=\.)\s+", doc)
sections, cur = [], []
for s in sentences:
    if len(s.split()) == 1 and cur:              # a one-word sentence like 'Refunds.' starts a new section
        sections.append(" ".join(cur)); cur = []
    cur.append(s)
sections.append(" ".join(cur))
print(f"structure-aware (by heading): {len(sections)} chunks")
for s in sections: print("  -", s)

# Reranking: a first-stage retriever returns candidates; a finer scorer re-orders them
q = "how many days until my refund arrives"
cands = sections + fixed(words, 12, 0)
def overlap(q, c): return len(set(re.findall(r"[a-z]+", q.lower())) & set(re.findall(r"[a-z]+", c.lower())))
first = sorted(cands, key=lambda c: -overlap(q, c))[:4]
def rerank(q, c):                                 # stand-in for a cross-encoder: rewards the key concept and the number of days
    s = overlap(q, c)
    s += 3 * ("refund" in c.lower()) + 1 * bool(re.search(r"\d+ days", c))
    return s
best = sorted(first, key=lambda c: -rerank(q, c))
print("\nfirst-stage top-1:", repr(first[0]))
print("after reranking  :", repr(best[0]))

prompt = ("Answer using only the context. If the answer is not there, say you don't know.\n"
          f"Context:\n[1] {best[0]}\nQuestion: {q}\nAnswer (cite [1]):")
print("\n" + prompt)

# Tabular RAG: turn the question into a filter/aggregation over a table instead of embedding rows as text
table = [{"city": "Pune", "quarter": "Q1", "sales": 120}, {"city": "Pune", "quarter": "Q2", "sales": 150},
         {"city": "Delhi", "quarter": "Q1", "sales": 200}, {"city": "Delhi", "quarter": "Q2", "sales": 140},
         {"city": "Chennai", "quarter": "Q2", "sales": 175}]
q2 = [r for r in table if r["quarter"] == "Q2"]
top = max(q2, key=lambda r: r["sales"])
print(f"\nQ: which city had the highest Q2 sales? -> filter quarter == Q2, argmax sales -> {top['city']} ({top['sales']})")
print(f"Q: total Pune sales? -> sum = {sum(r['sales'] for r in table if r['city'] == 'Pune')}")
